newsitem.title: UK: Bankers start Eurotunnel debt talks.
newsitem.headline: Bankers start Eurotunnel debt talks.

text.p: Bankers were meeting here on Friday to discuss Eurotunnel SA /Plc's financial restructuring plan agreed in principal earlier this week, the next rung on the ladder of getting the deal accepted by the creditors.
The six-strong steering committee will present the deal to the next tier of 26 "instructing banks" who represent the rest of Eurotunnel's 225 bank creditors.
"It's going to be mainly an information meeting at this stage although many participants will be very clear on what they can and cannot accept," said one banking source.

The steering committee reached agreement with Eurotunnel earlier this week on a restructuring plan designed to ensure the company's long-term future and reach a solution to its gargantuan nine billion pounds ($14 billion) debt.
Details of the deal are expected to be released on Monday when Eurotunnel holds news conferences in both Paris and London.
This is expected to lead to the return of Eurotunnel shares to the share markets from which they were suspended last Monday.

Analysts say around half of the firm's total debt must be retired in some way for the company to have a viable future and even then some feel it will still be a struggle depending largely on Eurotunnel's ability to raise prices while keeping market share on the cross-Channel route.

The deal is thought to contain a debt for equity swap of around 1.5 billion pounds which would leave the banks with 49 percent of the company's shares and a conversion of debt into a bond convertible into Eurotunnel shares.
This is thought to retire a further 2.0 to 2.5 billion pounds of debt and would, if converted, leave 70 percent of the company's shares in bank hands.
Bankers in London were displaying their customary caution ahead of Friday's meeting.

The general feeling is that, despite this week's understandable euphoria that a deal has been struck after a long year of talks, plenty of work still needs to be done to make sure the deal is not scuppered by unhappy creditors.
"Banks have different interests and problems," said one banker. "These all have to be accomodated and with so many in the group, it could be quite a job."
On the other hand, they feel that now that agreement is in view, both sides will want to keep up the momentum. ($1=.6388 Pound)
